overview: This card follows Pandya power and communities in southern Tamil country during the atlas’s 800 to 1000 interval. Ninth-century kings also extended their influence into the Kaveri region. The imported outline is seriously incomplete: it omits the capital Madurai and Sittannavasal, as well as that northern campaign area. Its dates are map slices, not the beginning and end of all Pandya history. Earlier Pandyas, later imperial Pandyas, Cholas and subsequent Madurai rulers have distinct histories.

periods.title: Ninth-century expansion and patronage
periods.summary: Temple donations record royal influence reaching into the Kaveri region.

periods.title: Chola intervention and changing rule
periods.summary: Early tenth-century Chola records celebrate victories over Pandya rulers; the atlas endpoint is not a single documented collapse.

sections.title: Kings, rivals and a damaged doorway

items.text: Valérie Gillet’s study connects thirty Kaveri-region inscriptions with Varaguna II. She identifies a thirteen-year period of Pandya sovereignty beginning in his fourth regnal year. Gifts to temples helped a conquering king establish relationships and display authority far from his southern center.

At Tiruccirrampalam, part of a Pandya donation survives on a sanctuary doorjamb. Gillet observed that people touching the doorway had rubbed away the middle of its text. Centuries of ordinary hands can erase words that a king expected stone to preserve.

An early tenth-century charter from Udayendiram praises the Chola king Parantaka I for taking Madurai, defeating the Pandya Rajasimha and repulsing an army from Sri Lanka. This is a rival court’s celebration of victory. It reveals serious political reversals, but its grand language should not be mistaken for a neutral battlefield report.

sections.title: A temple kitchen with an accountant

items.text: A ninth-century Tiruchendur inscription records a royal fund of 1,400 kasu. Officers were to preserve the principal and use its income for temple supplies. Worship required a practical financial system, with people responsible for turning an endowment into regular deliveries.

The supply list includes rice, plantains, sugar, vegetables and green pulse. Pepper, turmeric, cumin, mustard and coriander supplied seasoning. This is evidence for a temple kitchen, rather than every household’s menu, but the shopping list makes the past smell pleasantly like cooking.

One Tamil phrase is “kari tumikkavum porikkavum”, which the editor translates as “vegetable to be cut into pieces and fried”. It comes from line 26 of the ninth-century Tiruchendur inscription. These are published Latin transliterations of Vatteluttu writing, not modern Tamil letters or a complete recipe.

The same record budgets cloth for images and kitchen towels. Milk, curd and tender coconut water also appear, specifically for bathing the deity. Those ritual supplies do not establish ordinary people’s bathing habits, medical treatments or household toilets.

At Perungulam, Kudiyan Atulagunattan gave fifty sheep to support a temple lamp on behalf of his mother, Suvaran Achchi. Another inscription records his gift of a gong for his father, Maran Kudiyan. These early medieval records preserve family relationships through practical gifts of light and sound.

An Ambasamudram inscription describes Puvan Paraiyan buying fallow land from a village assembly, arranging irrigation and making it cultivable before endowing a temple. The gift involved more than handing over a field: someone had to bring water to previously unproductive ground.

At Kalugumalai, inscriptions attached to Jain images name teachers, disciples and donors. Women appear among the teachers, using titles such as kuratti. Donors came from several places across Tamil country. These records reveal networks of religious learning, although they do not describe a school timetable for every child.

A ninth-century inscription at Sittannavasal credits a teacher from Madurai with repairing the inner hall and adding a front mandapa under Srivallabha. Religious learning could go alongside organizing building work. This important site lies outside the atlas’s incomplete Pandya outline.

sections.title: Artists, books of metal and rediscovery

items.text: Look up at Sittannavasal’s painted ceiling and a lotus pond comes into view, with elephants and fish, including one leaping out of the water. The paintings belong to a Jain religious setting restored in the ninth century. Sacred art still leaves room for a very energetic fish.

Cleaning at Sittannavasal revealed that the ceiling had been painted twice. An underlying layer contained a carpet-like design. Conservators can therefore uncover changes in decoration, rather than assuming every surviving color was applied at once.

Kalugumalai’s reliefs include a woman dancing beside male musicians with stringed instruments, a drum and cymbals. Elsewhere, unfinished figures preserve stages in the stonecutters’ work. Owen generally places the Jain images in the ninth or early tenth century; the scenes are sacred art, not snapshots of a particular family party.

Pandya copper charters from the seventh to tenth centuries use Vatteluttu for Tamil and Grantha for Sanskrit. Sets of metal leaves could be held together by a ring. Some inscriptions have resurfaced during ploughing or building work: an old legal document can become an unexpected find in the ground.

ending.text: Chola victories reshaped Pandya rule during the tenth century. The atlas’s 1000 endpoint is not an extinction date. Later Pandya resurgence belongs to another phase.
